blocks.md: This lesson covers the book's section on **Fallacies and Pitfalls**. Read the excerpt, then test yourself below.

blocks.source: Vol III, Introduction, § Fallacies and Pitfalls
blocks.md: These three questions frame every mechanism in the book, and they also expose the common traps that appear when teams build or measure agents without them. A patch can compile cleanly without resolving the underlying defect, just as an agent can consume its turn budget without producing fresh evidence. Autonomous execution fails when system designers mistake churn inside the loop for genuine task completion.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Cost per accepted task matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: Under retry-until-accept, C_eff = E[C_attempt]/p_acc, so acceptance divides the whole attempt cost and any mechanism pays for its overhead only if it lowers this ratio.

questions.q: The section **Fallacies and Pitfalls** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Under retry-until-accept, C_eff = E[C_attempt]/p_acc, so acceptance divides the whole attempt cost and any mechanism pays for its overhead only if it lowers this ratio.
A trajectory that waits on a tool must decouple task lifetime from the serving allocation, or retained state occupies scarce memory while no tokens are produced.

A system is agentic when a runtime, not a human, closes the proposal-action-observation loop, so the model's output is a proposal with no standing authority and enforcement, isolation, persistence, and completion checks belong to the runtime.

Authority levels A0 to A3 (read-only, disposable workspace, compensable, irreversible) classify an action by its consequence in the environment, and the same command can change class when the environment changes.
